name: Cardinality
definition: Number of distinct values in a column (or relation size: number of rows).
why: Optimizer uses cardinality to choose joins, indexes, and broadcast vs shuffle.
example: `country` has ~200 distinct values (low cardinality). `user_id` may have millions (high cardinality).
remember: Low cardinality → bitmap indexes / dictionaries often help

name: Granularity (Grain)
definition: The level of detail one row represents (what one row means).
why: Wrong grain causes double-counting, bad joins, and incorrect metrics.
example: Orders table grain = one row per `order_id`. Order-items grain = one row per `order_id + product_id`.
remember: Never mix grains in one fact without care

name: Selectivity
definition: Fraction of rows a predicate returns. High selectivity = few rows (selective filter).
why: Selective predicates favor index seeks; low selectivity favors scans.
example: `WHERE user_id = 42` is highly selective. `WHERE status = 'active'` on 90% active rows is not.
remember: Indexes help most on selective filters

name: Data Distribution
definition: How values are spread across a column (uniform, skewed, sparse).
why: Skew causes hot partitions, slow joins, and uneven executor load.
example: 80% of orders from one country → that partition/key dominates shuffle.
remember: Salting and AQE help with skew

name: Histograms
definition: Statistics summarizing value frequency distribution in a column.
why: Help CBO estimate selectivity when values are uneven.
example: Optimizer sees `status='cancelled'` is 2% of rows via histogram, not assuming uniform 25%.

name: Cost-Based Optimizer (CBO)
definition: Chooses execution plan by estimating cost using table/column statistics.
why: Modern warehouses and Spark SQL rely on CBO for join order and strategies.
example: With stats, CBO picks broadcast hash join for a small dimension; without stats, may shuffle both sides.

name: Rule-Based Optimizer (RBO)
definition: Rewrites queries using fixed heuristic rules (e.g., push filters early), not cost estimates.
why: Fast and predictable; weak when data sizes vary.
example: Always push `WHERE` before `JOIN` regardless of table size.
remember: Spark Catalyst uses both rules and cost
RBO alone can miss better join strategies

name: Execution Plan
definition: The concrete operators the engine will run (scans, joins, aggregates, sorts).
why: Primary tool to debug slow queries.
example: Plan shows `SortMergeJoin` + large `Exchange` (shuffle) → expensive.
remember: Read bottom-up or follow arrows depending on engine

name: Explain Plan
definition: Command/API that prints the logical and/or physical plan without always running the full query.
why: Inspect strategy before/while tuning.
example:
```sql
EXPLAIN ANALYZE SELECT * FROM orders WHERE order_date = '2024-01-01';
-- Spark: df.explain(True)  or  EXPLAIN EXTENDED / COST
```

name: Composite Index
definition: Index on multiple columns in a defined order.
why: Speeds queries filtering/sorting on the leading columns.
example: Index `(customer_id, order_date)` helps `WHERE customer_id = ?` and `WHERE customer_id = ? AND order_date > ?`, not `WHERE order_date > ?` alone (usually).

name: Covering Index
definition: Index that contains all columns a query needs, so the table heap/base isn't touched.
why: Index-only scans are much faster for narrow queries.
example: Query selects `id, email` with index on `(id) INCLUDE (email)` → covering.
remember: Wider indexes cost more storage/write amp

name: Clustered vs Non-Clustered Index
definition: - **Clustered:** table rows stored in index key order (often primary key); typically one per table. - **Non-clustered:** separate structure pointing to rows; many allowed.
why: Clustered key choice affects range scans and insert patterns.
example: Clustered on `order_date` makes date-range queries fast; random UUIDs as clustered keys can fragment inserts.
remember: InnoDB PK is clustered; SQL Server similar
Choose clustered key for common access pattern

name: Bitmap Index
definition: Index storing bitmaps per distinct value; good for low-cardinality columns and AND/OR of predicates.
why: Common in analytic DBs; poor for high-churn OLTP updates.
example: Bitmap on `gender`, `region`, `status` for warehouse filters.

name: B-Tree Index
definition: Balanced tree index supporting equality and range lookups; default in most RDBMS.
why: Workhorse for OLTP and many warehouse lookups.
example: B-tree on `email` → fast `WHERE email = 'a@b.com'`.
remember: Not ideal alone for very low cardinality

name: Predicate Pushdown
definition: Move filters as close as possible to the data source so less data is read/shuffled.
why: Huge I/O and network savings on parquet/ORC and remote sources.
example: `spark.read.parquet(...).filter("year=2024")` pushes year filter into file/footer reading when partitioned.
remember: Prefer partition columns and columnar formats

name: Partition Pruning
definition: Skip reading partitions that cannot match the query filter.
why: Turns full scans into reading a fraction of data.
example: Table partitioned by `dt`; `WHERE dt='2024-06-01'` reads only that partition.

name: Statistics
definition: Metadata about tables/columns: row counts, NDV, min/max, histograms, size.
why: Fuel for CBO and good join strategies.

name: Table Scan vs Index Scan
definition: - **Table (full) scan:** read all rows/pages. - **Index scan:** walk an index (may still touch many rows).
why: Scans aren't always bad — for large fractions of the table they can win.
example: Selecting 2% of rows by PK → index. Selecting 70% → full scan often better.
remember: Optimizer picks based on selectivity + cost
"Index scan" ≠ cheap if it returns most of the table

name: Seek vs Scan
definition: - **Seek:** jump to a specific key/range in the index. - **Scan:** read a contiguous slice (or all) of index/table.
why: Seeks are for pinpoint lookups; scans for broader access.
example: `WHERE id = 10` → seek. `WHERE id BETWEEN 1 AND 1000000` → range scan.
remember: Large range scan can rival table scan

name: DAG Scheduler
definition: Builds a DAG of stages from the RDD/DataFrame lineage and submits stage tasks when parents finish.
why: Explains why shuffles create stage boundaries and how failures recompute.
example: `map → filter → reduceByKey` → narrow stage then shuffle stage.

name: Task Scheduler
definition: Assigns individual tasks to executors (resource offers from cluster manager).
why: Locality, speculation, and stragglers live here.
example: Prefer `PROCESS_LOCAL` / `NODE_LOCAL` tasks when data is cached on that executor.

name: Driver
definition: The process that runs your main program, builds the DAG, and coordinates executors.
why: Driver OOM or GC pauses stall the whole job.
example: Collecting a huge DataFrame to the driver (`collect()`) crashes the driver.
remember: Avoid large `collect` / broadcast of huge objects

name: Executor
definition: JVM worker process that runs tasks and stores shuffle/cache data.
why: Memory, cores, and disk per executor dominate performance.
example: 10 executors × 4 cores → up to 40 concurrent tasks.

name: Worker
definition: Cluster node process (e.g., Spark standalone worker) that hosts executors.
why: Distinguishes machine vs JVM process.
example: One worker machine runs multiple executors.

name: Cluster Manager
definition: Allocates resources: Standalone, YARN, Kubernetes, Mesos (legacy).
why: How cores/memory are requested and released.
example: `spark.master=yarn` or `k8s://...` with dynamic allocation.
remember: Dynamic allocation needs external shuffle service (classic YARN)

name: Job → Stage → Task
definition: - **Job:** triggered by an action (`count`, `write`, `collect`) - **Stage:** set of tasks with narrow deps between shuffles - **Task:** unit of work on one partition
why: UI debugging language.
example: One `write` action → 1 job → 3 stages → N tasks per stage.

name: Lineage
definition: Graph of transformations needed to recompute an RDD/DataFrame partition.
why: Fault tolerance without replicating all data.
example: Lose executor → recompute lost partitions from source + lineage.
remember: Lineage is logical, not always stored data

name: Lazy Evaluation
definition: Transformations build a plan; work runs only on actions.
why: Enables whole-stage optimization and predicate pushdown.
example: Many `filter`/`select` calls do nothing until `show()` or `write`.

name: Shuffle
definition: Redistribute data across partitions by key (network + sort/hash).
why: Usually the most expensive part of a job.
example: `groupBy`, `join`, `repartition`, `distinct` often shuffle.
remember: Watch shuffle read/write in Spark UI

name: Spill to Disk
definition: When memory is insufficient, intermediate data is written to local disk.
why: Correctness preserved; speed drops.
example: Large sort-merge join spills during sort.
remember: Spill ≠ failure; it's a warning sign
Increase memory, reduce partition size, or fix skew

name: Memory Management
definition: Spark splits executor memory among execution (shuffles/joins), storage (cache), and user/overhead.
why: Contention between cache and shuffle causes eviction/spill.
example: Unified memory region shared by execution and storage (post Spark 1.6).

name: Serialization (Java/Kryo)
definition: Convert objects to bytes for shuffle/cache/network. Kryo is faster/smaller than Java serializer when registered.
why: Slow serialization burns CPU on every shuffle.
example: `spark.serializer=org.apache.spark.serializer.KryoSerializer` + register classes.
remember: Prefer DataFrames (Catalyst/Tungsten) over RDDs of custom objects

name: Broadcast Variables
definition: Read-only copy of data sent once to each executor.
why: Avoids shipping large lookup tables per task.
example: Broadcast a small dimension for map-side join / `broadcast(df)`.
remember: Default auto-broadcast threshold exists in Spark SQL

name: Accumulators
definition: Write-only aggregate variables (counters) updated by executors, read on driver.
why: Lightweight metrics without collecting data.
example: Count malformed records while mapping.
remember: Updates inside transforms may be recomputed on retry — use carefully
Prefer built-in Spark metrics when possible

name: Closure
definition: Function + captured outer variables sent to executors.
why: Accidental capture of huge objects (DB connections, full DataFrames) causes OOM or slow shipping.
example: Capturing a large Python list in a UDF serializes it to every task.

name: Wide vs Narrow Transformations
definition: - **Narrow:** each input partition maps to ≤1 output partition (`map`, `filter`) — no shuffle - **Wide:** input partitions contribute to many outputs (`groupByKey`, `join`) — shuffle
why: Wide = stage boundary + cost.
example: `filter` narrow; `reduceByKey` wide.
remember: Pipeline narrow transforms in one stage

name: Adaptive Query Execution (AQE)
definition: Spark SQL re-optimizes the plan at runtime using size stats after shuffles (Spark 3+).
why: Fixes bad static estimates: coalesces partitions, switches join strategy, handles skew.
example: AQE converts sort-merge to broadcast when post-shuffle side is small.
remember: Helps skew join and partition coalescing

name: Catalyst Optimizer
definition: Spark SQL's rule + cost optimizer: analysis → logical optimization → physical planning.
why: Why DataFrames beat handwritten RDDs for SQL-like work.
example: Constant folding, predicate pushdown, column pruning done automatically.

name: Tungsten Engine
definition: Execution layer: off-heap/cache-aware memory, whole-stage codegen, binary processing.
why: Faster CPU and less GC than row-object RDDs.
example: Whole-stage codegen fuses operators into Java bytecode.
remember: Works best with native expressions (not Python UDFs)

name: Dynamic Partition Pruning
definition: At runtime, prune partitions of a large fact using values from a filtered dimension join.
why: Star-schema queries read far less data.
example: Join `sales` (partitioned by `date`) to `dim_date` filtered to one month → only those fact partitions scanned.
remember: Needs partitioned fact + filter on dimension

name: Skew Join Optimization
definition: Detect hot keys and split/handle them separately (AQE skew join, salting).
why: One key can stall an entire stage.
example: One `customer_id` with 40% of rows → AQE splits that partition.
remember: Check Spark UI for straggler tasks

name: Grain
definition: Exact meaning of one fact row (business level of detail).
why: Foundation of dimensional modeling; wrong grain breaks metrics.
example: "One row per order line per day" vs "one row per order".
remember: Declare grain in one sentence before designing
All measures must match that grain

name: Granularity
definition: Same idea as grain — how fine or coarse the data is. Often used interchangeably with grain in DW.
why: Aggregation level must match reporting needs.
example: Daily grain vs monthly rollup tables.
remember: Finer grain → more rows, more flexibility

name: Additive Facts
definition: Measures that can be summed across any dimension.
why: Safest metrics for rollups.
example: `sales_amount`, `quantity_sold` — sum by day, store, product all valid.

name: Semi-Additive Facts
definition: Summable across some dimensions, not others (often not across time).
why: Easy to misuse in BI (double-count balances).
example: Account balance — sum across customers OK; sum across days wrong (use last/average).
remember: Inventory and balances are classic semi-additive

name: Non-Additive Facts
definition: Cannot be summed meaningfully; ratios, percentages, temperatures.
why: Must recalculate from components, not average averages blindly.
example: `profit_margin` — store `profit` and `revenue`, compute margin at query time.

name: Degenerate Dimension
definition: Dimension-like identifier stored in the fact table with no separate dimension table.
why: Avoids empty dimension tables for transactional IDs.
example: `order_id`, `invoice_number` living on the fact row.

name: Junk Dimension
definition: Single dimension table combining low-cardinality flags/indicators.
why: Avoids many tiny dimensions cluttering the model.
example: `is_gift`, `payment_type`, `channel` packed into `dim_order_flags`.
remember: Good for yes/no and small enums

name: Role-Playing Dimension
definition: Same dimension reused for multiple roles via different foreign keys.
why: One `dim_date` serves order date, ship date, delivery date.
example: `order_date_key`, `ship_date_key` both point to `dim_date`.
remember: Views/aliases per role in BI tools

name: Conformed Dimension
definition: Shared dimension with consistent keys and attributes across facts/marts.
why: Enables cross-process drill-across reporting.
example: Same `customer_key` and customer attributes in sales and support marts.
remember: Owned by a shared data team/process

name: Mini Dimension
definition: Split frequently changing attributes into a smaller dimension to limit type-2 explosion on the main dim.
why: Keeps large customer dims manageable when demographics change often.
example: `dim_customer` stable attrs + `dim_customer_profile` for segment/score that changes monthly.
remember: Use when type-2 history would explode
Fact points to both keys when needed

name: Bridge Table
definition: Helper table resolving many-to-many between fact and dimension (or between dims).
why: Correct weighting and multi-valued attributes.
example: Order with multiple sales reps → `bridge_order_rep` with allocation weights.

name: Factless Fact Table
definition: Fact table with keys only (no numeric measures) — records events or coverage.
why: Answers "did it happen?" and "what was assigned?"
example: Student attendance: `student_key`, `class_key`, `date_key` — count rows = attendance events.
remember: Measures are often counts of rows

name: Snapshot Fact
definition: Fact capturing state at a point in time (generic term; often periodic).
why: Measures levels (balances, inventory) over time.
example: Daily inventory on-hand per SKU per warehouse.

name: Accumulating Snapshot
definition: One row per process instance; columns updated as milestones complete (pipeline pipeline).
why: Tracks lifecycle duration and conversion.
example: Order fulfillment: `ordered_at`, `packed_at`, `shipped_at`, `delivered_at` on one row, updated in place.

name: Periodic Snapshot
definition: New fact rows taken at regular intervals for all entities (day/week/month).
why: Time-series of levels for reporting.
example: End-of-day account balance for every account every day.
remember: Storage heavy but query-friendly for trends

name: Data Lake
definition: Central storage of raw and processed data in files (often object storage), schema-on-read.
why: Cheap scale for diverse data; weak governance if unmanaged.
example: S3/ADLS/GCS buckets with landing, bronze, silver zones as folders.
remember: Needs catalog, quality, and access control

name: Data Lakehouse
definition: Lake storage + warehouse capabilities: ACID tables, governance, BI-friendly SQL.
why: One copy of data for batch, streaming, and analytics.
example: Delta/Iceberg tables on S3 queried by Spark, Trino, and BI tools.
remember: Open table formats are the core
Combines lake cost with warehouse reliability

name: Delta Lake
definition: Open table format (Databricks-origin) with transaction log (`_delta_log`) for ACID on files.
why: Upserts, time travel, schema enforcement on object storage.
example: `MERGE INTO target USING source ON ... WHEN MATCHED THEN UPDATE ...`
remember: Transaction log is source of truth

name: Apache Iceberg
definition: Open table format with snapshot metadata, hidden partitioning, strong engine interoperability.
why: Multi-engine lakehouse (Spark, Flink, Trino, Athena).
example: Partition evolution without rewriting all data paths visible to users.
remember: Hidden partitioning is a key feature

name: Apache Hudi
definition: Open table format focused on incremental processing, upserts, and streaming ingestion.
why: Near-real-time lakes with copy-on-write or merge-on-read.
example: Upsert CDC into a Hudi MOR table; readers see compacted view.
remember: COW vs MOR tradeoffs (write vs read cost)

name: Time Travel
definition: Query table as of a past version/timestamp via snapshots/logs.
why: Reproduce reports, debug bad writes, audit.
example:
```sql
SELECT * FROM orders VERSION AS OF 120;
-- or TIMESTAMP AS OF '2024-06-01'
```
remember: Great for "what did we have yesterday?"

name: Schema Evolution
definition: Safely change table schema (add/rename/drop columns) without full reload when supported.
why: Pipelines and producers change over time.
example: Adding `discount_code` column to a Delta/Iceberg table.

name: Schema Enforcement
definition: Reject writes that don't match the table schema (or strict evolution rules).
why: Stops corrupt/partial schemas from poisoning the lake.
example: Write with extra unexpected type fails instead of silently creating junk files.

name: ACID Tables
definition: Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation, Durability for table operations on the lake.
why: Readers never see partial commits; concurrent writers coordinated.
example: A failed job leaves no half-visible partition after transactional commit.
remember: File formats alone aren't ACID — table formats add it
Isolation level still matters for readers

name: Compaction
definition: Rewrite many small files into larger optimized files.
why: Fixes small-file problem; improves scan speed.
example: Iceberg rewrite / Hudi compact / Delta OPTIMIZE.
remember: Trade compute now for faster reads later

name: Vacuum
definition: Delete obsolete data files no longer referenced by the table (past retention).
why: Reclaims storage; ends time-travel past retention.
example: `VACUUM table_name RETAIN 168 HOURS;` (Delta).
remember: Too aggressive vacuum breaks time travel / long readers

name: Optimize
definition: Maintenance command to compact/layout data for faster reads (Delta `OPTIMIZE`).
why: Combines small files; optional Z-Order clustering.
example: `OPTIMIZE sales ZORDER BY (customer_id, event_date);`
remember: Run on tables with heavy small-file ingest

name: Z-Ordering
definition: Multi-dimensional clustering of data files so related values co-locate (minmax skipping improves).
why: Faster filters on high-cardinality columns that aren't partition keys.
example: Z-Order by `user_id` so point lookups skip most files.
remember: Complement to partitioning, not a replacement

name: CAP Theorem
definition: In a network partition, a system can provide Consistency or Availability, not both (Partition tolerance assumed in distributed DBs).
why: Forces explicit tradeoffs in data platforms.
example: During partition, CP system rejects writes; AP system accepts writes that may conflict.
remember: Real systems tune the C/A tradeoff
"CA without P" isn't realistic for multi-node

name: BASE
definition: Basically Available, Soft state, Eventually consistent — alternative mindset to strict ACID across distributed services.
why: Many large-scale stores and caches lean BASE.
example: Shopping cart eventually syncs across regions; brief stale reads OK.
remember: Soft state may change without input (anti-entropy)

name: Eventual Consistency
definition: If no new updates, all replicas converge to the same value eventually.
why: Default for many geo-replicated and highly available systems.
example: Read-after-write may fail briefly across regions; later reads agree.
remember: Use stronger reads when needed (quorum/linearizable APIs)

name: Strong Consistency
definition: After a write commits, all subsequent reads see it (linearizability / similar guarantees vary by system).
why: Simpler app logic; higher latency/cost.
example: Financial ledger balance must be strongly consistent.
remember: Costs latency and availability under partitions

name: Replication
definition: Keep multiple copies of data for durability and/or read scale.
why: Failure domains and read throughput.
example: Kafka topic RF=3; Postgres primary + replicas; S3 cross-region copy.

name: Leader Election
definition: Cluster chooses a primary coordinator for writes or decisions.
why: Avoids split-brain conflicting writes.
example: ZooKeeper/etcd/Raft elect Kafka controller or DB primary.
remember: Fencing tokens prevent old leaders writing

name: Consensus
definition: Nodes agree on a value/order of operations despite failures.
why: Metadata, configs, and transaction logs need agreement.
example: Agreeing on the next committed Kafka controller epoch or Raft log entry.

name: Raft
definition: Consensus algorithm emphasizing understandability: leader, log replication, terms.
why: Used by etcd, Consul, many modern systems.
example: etcd stores K8s state via Raft.

name: Paxos
definition: Classic family of consensus protocols (Multi-Paxos, etc.).
why: Theoretical foundation; still in older systems (Chubby-like).
example: Google Chubby historically influenced by Paxos.
remember: Harder to implement correctly than Raft

name: Fault Tolerance
definition: System continues correctly despite component failures.
why: Commodity hardware fails; jobs and stores must survive.
example: Spark recomputes lost partitions; Kafka replicates partitions.

name: High Availability (HA)
definition: Minimize downtime via redundancy and fast failover.
why: SLAs for pipelines and serving layers.
example: Multi-AZ brokers; standby scheduler; health checks + auto restart.
remember: HA ≠ zero data loss (depends on durability config)

name: Horizontal Scaling
definition: Add more nodes to increase capacity.
why: Default for big data systems.
example: Add Spark executors or Kafka brokers.

name: Vertical Scaling
definition: Give one machine more CPU/RAM/disk.
why: Simple until limits/cost/HA constraints hit.
example: Upsize a warehouse warehouse node or driver machine.
remember: Ceiling exists; single point of failure risk
Mix: scale out data plane, scale up hot coordinators carefully

name: Event Time
definition: Timestamp when the event actually occurred in the real world.
why: Correct windows despite late/out-of-order arrival.
example: Click happened at 10:00; arrived at 10:07 → event time = 10:00.
remember: Prefer event time for analytics windows

name: Processing Time
definition: Time on the machine when the event is processed.
why: Simple but wrong for delayed data.
example: Same click processed at 10:07 → processing-time window uses 10:07.

name: Ingestion Time
definition: Time when the event enters the streaming system.
why: Middle ground; stable clock at entry, not true event time.
example: Kafka timestamp at produce/consume (depending on config).
remember: Better than processing time for some cases
Still not true business event time

name: Watermarks
definition: Engine's notion of how far event time has advanced; used to close windows.
why: Trade completeness vs latency for late data.
example: Watermark = max_event_time - 10 minutes → close hour window when watermark passes end + grace.

name: Windowing
definition: Group stream events into finite buckets: tumbling, sliding, session.
why: Aggregations need bounded scopes.
example: Tumbling 5-min count of orders; session window by user inactivity gap.

name: Late Data
definition: Events arriving after the watermark/window allowed them.
why: Reality of mobile/offline producers.
example: Event time 10:01 arrives at 10:25 with 5-min watermark — late.
remember: Side outputs / allowed lateness / update previous results

name: Stateful Processing
definition: Operators keep state across events (windows, joins, dedupe).
why: Enables real aggregations; needs checkpointing and TTL.
example: Running count per user; stream-stream join.

name: Stateless Processing
definition: Each event handled independently; no cross-event state.
why: Easier scale and recovery.
example: Map parse JSON → enrich from broadcast config → filter.

name: Exactly Once
definition: Effect of each record applied once end-to-end (despite retries).
why: No double-counting in sinks.
example: Kafka → Flink → transactional sink / idempotent sink with checkpoints.
remember: "Exactly once" is end-to-end, not just processing

name: At Least Once
definition: Every record processed ≥1 time; duplicates possible on retry.
why: Common default; simpler than exactly-once.
example: Restart after crash reprocesses last uncommitted batch.

name: At Most Once
definition: Process ≤1 time; may lose data on failure.
why: Lowest latency/complexity; rare for critical pipelines.
example: Fire metrics where loss is acceptable.

name: Event Sourcing
definition: Persist state as an append-only sequence of events; rebuild state by replay.
why: Auditability and temporal queries.
example: `OrderPlaced`, `ItemAdded`, `OrderShipped` rebuild current order.

name: CQRS
definition: Command Query Responsibility Segregation — separate write model from read model(s).
why: Scale reads/writes independently; tailor projections.
example: Write orders to OLTP; project read-optimized order search index.
remember: Read models can be eventually consistent

name: Idempotency
definition: Running the same operation multiple times yields the same result as running once.
why: Retries and backfills won't duplicate or corrupt data.
example: Upsert by primary key; overwrite partition `dt=2024-01-01` instead of append-only blindly.

name: Checkpointing
definition: Persist progress (offsets/state) so recovery resumes cleanly.
why: Fault-tolerant streaming and long batch stages.
example: Spark Structured Streaming checkpoint location stores offsets + state.
remember: Checkpoint path is critical state — back it up/protect it
Changing query identity may invalidate checkpoints

name: Retry Strategy
definition: Policy for re-attempting failed work (how many, when, which errors).
why: Transient cloud/network faults are normal.
example: Retry S3/API 429/5xx up to 5 times; fail fast on 400 auth errors.
remember: Cap retries to avoid thundering herds

name: Backoff Strategy
definition: Increase wait between retries (often exponential + jitter).
why: Prevents stampeding a recovering dependency.
example: Wait 1s, 2s, 4s, 8s with random jitter.

name: Circuit Breaker
definition: Stop calling a failing dependency temporarily after error threshold; probe later.
why: Fails fast; protects both sides from cascade.
example: After 50 warehouse connection failures, open circuit for 60s, then half-open trial.

name: Dead Letter Queue (DLQ)
definition: Side channel for records that fail processing after retries.
why: Unblocks the main pipeline; enables quarantine and replay.
example: Malformed JSON → DLQ topic/table with error reason; alert and fix.

name: Data Contracts
definition: Explicit agreement on schema, semantics, SLAs, and ownership between producers and consumers.
why: Prevents silent breaking changes.
example: Producer guarantees `orders.v2` fields + daily freshness < 2h; CI validates schema.
remember: Enforce in CI/CD and at write time

name: Pipeline Orchestration
definition: Schedule, dependency management, retries, and observability of multi-step data jobs.
why: Production reliability beyond a single script.
example: Airflow/Dagster/Prefect/Azure DF: extract → transform → test → publish.
remember: Prefer data-aware sensors over blind cron when possible

name: Metadata-Driven Pipelines
definition: Behavior configured by metadata (tables, mappings, rules) rather than hard-coded per table jobs.
why: Scales to hundreds of similar pipelines.
example: Config table lists source, target, PK, SCD type → one generic loader.
remember: Keep escape hatches for special cases

name: Data Skew
definition: Uneven key/partition sizes so a few tasks do most of the work.
why: Stage time ≈ slowest task.
example: `null` or popular `country_code` holds 50% of join keys.
remember: Fix with salting, AQE skew join, or pre-agg

name: Broadcast Join
definition: Replicate the small side to all executors; join locally (map-side).
why: Avoids shuffling the large side.
example: Fact × small dimension (`broadcast(dim)`).

name: Shuffle Join
definition: Generic term for joins that redistribute both sides by join key (often sort-merge or shuffle-hash).
why: Expensive but necessary for two large tables.
example: Large `orders` ⋈ large `payments` on `order_id`.
remember: Ensure join keys have good distribution

name: Sort Merge Join
definition: Shuffle both sides by key, sort, then merge — Spark's common large-large join.
why: Scalable; sensitive to skew and spill.
example: Default for two big DataFrames when broadcast isn't chosen.

name: Hash Join
definition: Build hash table on one side, probe with the other (in-memory or spilled).
why: Fast when build side fits (or partially).
example: Broadcast hash join = hash join with replicated build side.

name: Bucket Join
definition: Tables pre-bucketed (and often sorted) on the same key so joins avoid full shuffle.
why: Speeds repeated joins on stable keys.
example: Both tables bucketed by `user_id` into 200 buckets → bucket join.
remember: Bucket count must match (or be compatible)
Worth it for heavy reuse patterns

name: Salting
definition: Add a random salt to hot keys to spread them across partitions, then remove/aggregate.
why: Manual skew fix when AQE isn't enough.
example: Hot `customer_id` → `customer_id + salt_0..N` on both sides for join, then drop salt.
remember: Choose salt range from skew severity

name: Caching
definition: Keep a dataset in memory/disk across actions to avoid recomputation.
why: Iterative algorithms and multi-action reuse.
example: `df.cache()` before multiple joins/aggregations on same base.

name: Persistence Levels
definition: Storage level for cached data: memory only, memory+disk, disk only, serialized, replicated.
why: Trade speed vs memory pressure vs reliability.
example: `MEMORY_AND_DISK` safer than `MEMORY_ONLY` for large frames.

name: Parallelism
definition: Degree of concurrent tasks (related to partitions and cores).
why: Too low = idle cluster; too high = scheduling overhead.
example: `repartition(200)` to use ~200 cores effectively for a stage.
remember: Target a few partitions per core
Aim for reasonable partition file sizes

name: Partition Sizing
definition: Choosing number/size of partitions (and output files) for balanced work.
why: Core lever for Spark/Hive performance.
example: Target ~128–256 MB per partition file for many lake workloads (rule of thumb, not law).

name: Small File Problem
definition: Too many tiny files → heavy listing, task overhead, slow queries.
why: Streaming/micro-batch ingest often creates this.
example: 100k files of 1 MB instead of 400 files of 256 MB.

name: Data Profiling
definition: Statistical survey of a dataset: nulls, distincts, distributions, patterns.
why: Baseline before modeling and for anomaly detection.
example: 12% null `email`; `amount` min/max/p99; top values of `status`.

name: Data Validation
definition: Automated checks that data meets rules (schema, ranges, uniqueness, referential).
why: Catch bad data before it hits consumers.
example: Great Expectations / dbt tests: `order_id` unique, `amount >= 0`, FK to customers.
remember: Fail or quarantine on critical rules

name: Data Lineage
definition: Trace where data came from and where it flows (table/column/job level).
why: Impact analysis, debugging, compliance.
example: `raw.orders` → `stg_orders` → `fct_orders` → dashboard KPI.
remember: Column-level lineage is gold for audits

name: Metadata
definition: Data about data: schema, owners, freshness, partitions, descriptions.
why: Discoverability and safe use.
example: Table description, column glossary, last update time, PII tags.
remember: Stale metadata is worse than none if trusted blindly

name: Data Catalog
definition: Searchable inventory of datasets with metadata, ownership, and often lineage.
why: "Where is customer revenue defined?"
example: DataHub, Collibra, Unity Catalog, Glue Data Catalog, OpenMetadata.

name: Master Data Management (MDM)
definition: Processes/systems to create a single trusted master for core entities (customer, product).
why: Deduped golden records across systems.
example: Merge CRM + billing customers into golden `customer_id` with survivorship rules.

name: Data Governance
definition: Policies, roles, and controls for data quality, security, privacy, and usage.
why: Trust, compliance (GDPR etc.), consistent definitions.
example: PII classification, access reviews, approved metric definitions.
remember: Embed in pipelines, not only documents

name: Data Stewardship
definition: Human ownership of domain data quality and definitions.
why: Governance without stewards doesn't stick.
example: Finance steward owns `revenue` definition and approves changes.

name: Observability
definition: Ability to understand pipeline health via metrics, logs, traces, and data checks.
why: Detect silent data failures, not just job crashes.
example: Freshness, row-count anomalies, schema drift alerts, job duration SLOs.
remember: Alert on symptoms that matter to consumers

name: Freshness
definition: How up-to-date the data is vs expectation (SLA/SLO).
why: Stale dashboards mislead decisions.
example: "Orders table max `updated_at` < 1 hour ago".
remember: Alert on breach, not only job fail

name: Completeness
definition: Required data is present (rows and fields).
why: Missing partitions/nulls break KPIs.
example: All 24 hourly partitions arrived; `customer_id` null rate < 0.1%.

name: Accuracy
definition: Data correctly represents real-world values.
why: Valid schema can still be wrong.
example: Currency conversion rates match source system within tolerance.

name: Consistency
definition: Same facts agree across systems/tables within defined rules.
why: Conflicting numbers destroy trust.
example: Sum of order lines equals order header total; warehouse matches finance extract.
remember: Define which system is source of truth

name: Object Storage
definition: Store immutable objects (files) addressed by key in buckets; virtually infinite scale.
why: Default substrate for data lakes.
example: S3, ADLS Gen2, GCS holding parquet/Delta tables.
remember: Eventually consistent listing quirks are rarer now but design carefully

name: Block Storage
definition: Disk volumes attached to VMs (like SAN/local disks).
why: Databases, Kafka brokers, Spark local shuffle disks.
example: EBS/Azure Disks for Postgres data directory.

name: Lifecycle Policies
definition: Automatic transition/expire of objects by age/prefix (hot → cool → archive → delete).
why: Cost control for lakes and logs.
example: Raw logs to Glacier after 90 days; delete after 365.

name: IAM
definition: Identity and Access Management — who can do what on which resources.
why: Security boundary for every cloud data platform.
example: Role for Spark job: read `s3://lake/bronze/*`, write `s3://lake/silver/*` only.

name: Secrets Management
definition: Store/rotate credentials and API keys outside code.
why: Prevent leaks in repos and logs.
example: AWS Secrets Manager / Azure Key Vault / HashiCorp Vault for DB passwords.

name: KMS
definition: Key Management Service — create and control encryption keys.
why: Separate permission to use keys from permission to see data.
example: S3 SSE-KMS; revoke key usage to lock data access.

name: Encryption at Rest
definition: Data encrypted on disk/storage media.
why: Protects against disk theft and some breach scenarios.
example: S3 default encryption; encrypted EBS volumes.

name: Encryption in Transit
definition: Data encrypted on the network (TLS/HTTPS).
why: Protects against eavesdropping on the wire.
example: TLS to warehouses, HTTPS to APIs, SSL to Postgres.

name: VPC
definition: Virtual Private Cloud — isolated network for your cloud resources.
why: Network security and private connectivity.
example: Data platform subnets with no public IPs; NAT for egress.
remember: Control egress for cost and security

name: Private Endpoints
definition: Private network interfaces to cloud services without public internet.
why: Keep data plane traffic off public network.
example: S3/GCP Private Service Connect / Azure Private Link to storage and warehouses.
remember: Prefer for production lake + warehouse access

name: Docker
definition: Package app + dependencies into portable container images.
why: Same Spark/Python job runs locally, CI, and prod.
example: Image with `spark-submit` entrypoint and pinned library versions.
remember: Pin base image digests for reproducibility
Keep images lean; separate build vs runtime if needed

name: Kubernetes
definition: Orchestrates containers: scheduling, scaling, restarts, service discovery.
why: Common runtime for Spark-on-K8s, Airflow, Flink, microservices.
example: SparkApplication CRD submits driver/executors as pods.

name: CI/CD
definition: Continuous Integration / Continuous Delivery — automate test and deploy of code/config.
why: Safe, repeatable pipeline and dbt/SQL changes.
example: PR runs unit tests + SQL lint → merge deploys DAG to Airflow.
remember: Separate deploy of code vs heavy data backfills

name: GitOps
definition: Desired system state lives in Git; controllers sync cluster to match.
why: Auditable infra and app deploys.
example: Argo CD applies Helm charts from `infra` repo on merge to main.

name: Terraform
definition: Declarative Infrastructure as Code tool (HCL) for cloud resources.
why: Reproducible buckets, IAM, warehouses, networks.
example: Terraform creates S3 lake buckets, Glue catalog DB, IAM roles.

name: Helm
definition: Package manager for Kubernetes — charts template K8s manifests.
why: Standard way to deploy Airflow, Spark operator, monitoring stacks.
example: `helm upgrade --install airflow bitnami/airflow -f values.yaml`.

name: Infrastructure as Code (IaC)
definition: Define and version infrastructure in code (Terraform, CloudFormation, Pulumi, Bicep).
why: Repeatable environments; peer-reviewed changes.
example: Dev/stage/prod lakes created from the same modules with different variables.
remember: Codify networking, IAM, and data stores together
